tech: How technical the clothes are. Depth of technical product drives the scale; who owns the technology decides only whether a house can reach the top. A membrane keeps the rain out whoever holds the patent, so a house selling licensed Gore-Tex is selling technical clothing, and a house selling stock stretch polyester under its own fabric names is selling a milder version of the same thing. 5 is reserved for a house that developed what it sells. 4 is a range as technical, bought in — licensed like Sease’s Loro Piana Storm System, or commodity performance cloth carrying house names, as Peter Millar’s Summer Comfort is 92% polyester with spandex. 3 is a real but partial technical business. 1 is a trace. Vollebak names no technology at all and takes a 5: the material is the name, and the house went and found the graphene.
comfort: How central softness and physical ease are to what the brand sells — fiber, stretch, drape, wash. 5 = comfort is the entire pitch.
craft: Verifiable making: who makes it, where, and for how long — owned factories, named mills, documented process, heritage with receipts. 5 = the maker and the brand are the same thing.
style: How much the brand trades on design point of view and fashion influence rather than perfected basics. 5 = the look is the reason it exists.
fuss: Two-way, measuring what the garment asks of you — not durability, and not fabric technology. Performance fabric usually asks more, not less: cold wash, hang dry, no softener, periodic reproofing. Cotton duck and jersey ask nothing. Left is easy, right is demanding. −3 effortless — hot wash, tumble dry, never press. −1 simple. 0 normal. +1 some care — a specific routine, quick but non-negotiable, where most technical kit sits. +3 specialist care. Derived from each brand's fabric profile, with overrides where fabric cannot see the whole story — Barbour is +3 on re-waxing while scoring nothing on Tech.
dur: How long the garment survives being used. Independent of both care and price — a $650 hoodie is no more durable than a $60 one, and heavy cotton outlasts fine wool. 5 = outlives you and is meant to; repairable, and the maker expects you to. 4 = built heavy, expected to last. 3 = solid, ordinary lifespan. 2 = fine gauge or delicate, or built for a season. 0 = not assessed.
forg: How closely you can land on your own body. Two things: cut tolerance — whether the garment forgives a body that is not the fit model's — and precision, meaning how finely you can specify. Waist × inseam rather than S/M/L; in-between sizes; separate lengths; slim, classic and relaxed offered in the same size; made-to-measure at the top end. Extended sizing is deliberately excluded: stocking to 5XL is about who can buy the brand at all, which is a different question. NOTE: scores currently reflect an earlier version of this rubric that weighted extended sizing, and are being re-verified against live product pages.
denim: How central denim is to the brand's identity. 1 = incidental. 5 = a denim house first — delete the jeans and the company disappears.
cashmere: How central cashmere is to the brand's identity. 1 = incidental. 5 = the company is built on the fiber and wouldn't survive without it.
linen: How central linen is to the brand's identity. 1 = incidental. 5 = linen is the founding material.
cotton: Premium cotton as identity — long-staple fiber, Supima or Sea Island programs, signature jersey. 5 = the brand's reputation rests on its cotton.
wool: Wool as identity — tailoring cloth, merino, Shetland, flannel. 5 = a wool house, with the mills and suiting at the core.
synth: Performance synthetics and technical blends as identity. 5 = built on engineered fabric.
golf: 5 = the pro shop is the native habitat. 4 = clubhouse staple. 3 = country-club lifestyle. 2 = owns a golf line or shows up on course. 1 = stopped at the starter's shack.
status: Signal power to the audience the wearer is dressing for — loud logos and quiet insider cues both count. 5 = the garment does the talking. 1 = signals nothing, often on purpose.
finbro: How central the brand is to the American finance uniform. 5 = the uniform itself — the vest, the quarter-zip. 4 = standard issue at some rank of the career. 1 = has never seen a pitch deck.
ivy: How central to the American campus-trad canon and its lineage. 5 = source material — the campus clothiers and the empire built from them. 4 = the revival's major houses. 1 = no crest, no quad.
prep: The lifestyle uniform — club decks, coastal weekends, go-to-hell pants. Distinct from Ivy League: Ivy is the collegiate source canon; Prep is the whole way of life. 5 = the uniform itself; 3 = fluent; 1 = never joined the club.
murica: How loudly the brand reads as American — iconography, mythology, and roots. 5 = the flag is practically a material. 1 = another country's story. Actual US manufacturing helps but doesn't decide it.
ital: How much Italy carries the brand — Italian make, Italian mills, Italian design language. Passport not required: American brands with Italian factories and cloth score, while Italian brands selling an American fantasy score lower than you'd think. 5 = Italy is the argument itself.
fren: How much France carries the brand — Parisian codes, Riviera sun, or Place Vendôme institution; the effortlessness doctrine counts as much as the address. 5 = France is the argument. Mirror cases score both ways: Moncler was born French-alpine and naturalized Italian.
street: How native the brand is to street culture — sneakers, drops, skate and hip-hop lineage. 5 = the street is the source; 4 = fluent; 3 = adopted by the street, or borrowing from it; 1 = never touched pavement.
avant: How far the brand pushes against clothing's conventions — silhouette, construction, concept, presentation. 5 = an ongoing argument with clothing itself; 4 = radical form you can wear to dinner; 3 = a foot in the gallery; 1 = clothes as clothes.
weird: How gleefully strange the design output is — pigeon clutches, tabi toes, jackets for Mars. Distinct from Avant-Garde: avant argues with clothing; weird just delights in oddity. 5 = the odd is the brand; 3 = a streak of strange; 1 = plays it straight.
boat: Which deck the clothes are cut for, by boat length. 1 = a 25ft centre console you drive yourself, cooler in the bow. 2 = a 35-40ft weekender, you know the lines. 3 = 50-60ft, blazer at the club afterwards. 4 = 80-120ft crewed, linen and no visible logos. 5 = 200ft+, cashmere on deck in July. 0 = no boat. Unlike the other registers this is a tier, not an adoption score — it asks which deck, not how nautical.
racquet: Which court the clothes are cut for, least to most fancy. 1 = pickleball, public court. 2 = municipal tennis or padel, booked online. 3 = country-club tennis. 4 = private club grass or clay, whites enforced. 5 = squash, members-only — the court is a building, not a surface, so a club owns it. 0 = no court. Like Boat this is a tier, not an adoption score.
briish: How much Britain carries the brand — the mills, the shop lineage, the country-and-club wardrobe, or London's design school. A passport is neither required nor sufficient: a Neapolitan house softening an English jacket scores, and a London address selling something else does not. 5 = Britain is the argument; 3 = fluent; 1 = a trace.
scandi: How much the brand belongs to the Nordic design tradition — restraint, function, a muted palette and democratic design. A geographic register, like italianness and frenchness: Nordic origin is what gets a house onto the dial, and the score then asks how much of the tradition it actually trades in. A Swedish house selling English shirt formality scores low; a non-Nordic house working the same register scores at most a 2, because the dial is about where a house comes from as well as how it designs. 5 = the tradition is the argument; 3 = fluent; 1 = a trace.
ski: How much the mountain runs the brand. 5 = the slope is the founding brief and still current. 4 = a serious ski programme inside a broader technical house. 3 = a real ski line rather than a capsule. 2 = a capsule, an après register, or a historic association. 1 = a trace. 0 = no mountain. Unlike Boat and Racquet this is an adoption score, not a tier — it asks how much, not which slope.
